```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(cluster)

options(bdat602.source_only = TRUE)
source("courses/bdat-602/_teacher/resources/datasets/simulate_bdat602_data.R")
health_data <- simulate_bdat602(n = 5000, seed = 602)
```

## Task 1: Prepare the data

```{r task1-prepare}
clust_data <- health_data |>
  select(age, bmi, income, num_claims, num_chronic_conditions) |>
  drop_na() |>
  scale()

dim(clust_data)
```

## Task 2: Fit hierarchical clustering (Ward linkage) and plot the dendrogram

```{r task2-hclust}
D  <- dist(clust_data, method = "euclidean")
hc <- hclust(D, method = "ward.D2")

plot(hc, labels = FALSE, hang = -1,
     main = "Ward.D2 Dendrogram — Insurance Policyholders",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
abline(h = 30, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

```{r task2-interpret}
# The dendrogram shows two main branches merging at the top (~height 60-80).
# Each branch splits further into sub-branches.
# Cutting at h ≈ 30 separates the tree into approximately 4 groups,
# which corresponds to the elbow k identified in the k-means lesson.
```

## Task 3: Extract clusters and compare to k-means

```{r task3-cutree}
clusters_hc <- cutree(hc, k = 4)
table(clusters_hc)
```

```{r task3-compare}
set.seed(602)
km4 <- kmeans(clust_data, centers = 4, nstart = 25)

cat("Hierarchical cluster sizes:", table(clusters_hc), "\n")
cat("k-means cluster sizes:     ", km4$size, "\n")

# Ward hierarchical clustering often produces more balanced cluster sizes than
# k-means because Ward's merge criterion directly minimises variance increase
# (analogous to k-means objective), making the two methods produce similar results.
# k-means cluster sizes tend to vary more due to random initialisation effects.
```

## Task 4: Single linkage — chaining effect

```{r task4-single-linkage}
hc_single <- hclust(D, method = "single")

plot(hc_single, labels = FALSE, hang = -1,
     main = "Single Linkage Dendrogram — Insurance Policyholders",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
```

```{r task4-chaining}
clusters_single <- cutree(hc_single, k = 4)
table(clusters_single)

# The single linkage dendrogram is characteristic: one giant cluster grows by
# absorbing individual points one at a time (chaining), rather than merging
# two similarly-sized sub-clusters. Extracting k = 4 clusters typically gives
# one cluster with ~4,990+ members and 3 clusters with only 1-2 members.
# This is the "chaining effect": single linkage cannot produce compact,
# balanced clusters because it always links via the nearest pair of points,
# not the nearest pair of cluster centroids.
# Ward linkage avoids this by penalising increases in within-cluster variance.
```
